title: Job Scheduler
summary: Run one-off and cron jobs on time with sharded schedulers that claim due jobs with leases, a priority queue and idempotent, at-least-once Workers.
narrative:
Let users submit jobs that run once at a time T or on a cron schedule, with priorities and retries. Jobs must start on time — within ~1 s — and must never be lost. Plan for ~100 M scheduled jobs and ~10 K runs/s at peak, because cron schedules cluster at the top of each hour, ~10× the average of ~1 K runs/s. On a single machine this is simple: keep jobs in a min-heap ordered by next run time, let a timer thread sleep until the earliest job is due, and hand due jobs to a worker pool; a new job due sooner than the current earliest wakes the timer. The distributed design keeps the same roles — an ordered list of due times, a scheduler and workers — but makes each one durable and replicated.

Clients call the job API through a Load Balancer and Web Servers, which store job definitions, next_run_time and run history in the SQL Database, indexed by next_run_time. Several Task Scheduler instances each own a shard of the jobs; shard ownership and leader election come from a coordination service such as ZooKeeper / etcd, so when one scheduler dies its shards move to another. Each scheduler repeatedly claims the jobs in its shards that are due in the next few seconds with a lease: a conditional update that sets claimed_by and lease_until only if the job is unclaimed or its lease has expired. One scheduler holds a job at a time, and if a scheduler stalls past its lease another may claim the job again, which is one more reason runs must be idempotent. The scheduler keeps its claimed jobs in an in-memory min-heap — the single-machine design again — pushes each run to a Message Queue with separate priority lanes when it falls due, and advances next_run_time for recurring jobs. A job submitted with a due time sooner than the next polling window is handed by the Web Server straight to a Task Scheduler, which claims it the same way, instead of waiting for the next poll.

Workers pull runs from the queue, execute them idempotently, keyed by job id and scheduled time, and record each run's status in SQL; a failed run is retried with exponential backoff by setting its next attempt time. Delivery is at least once: a run whose Worker dies is re-delivered when its visibility timeout or lease expires, so a job may occasionally run twice but is never lost. Runs that keep failing land in a Dead Letter Queue for inspection. Many jobs due at the same moment are absorbed by the queue while Workers autoscale on its depth. Optionally add Monitoring for schedule lag, queue depth and failures.

functional: Submit one-off jobs for a time T and recurring cron jobs, each with a priority and a retry policy
Store job definitions, next_run_time and run history in SQL
Claim due jobs in each scheduler's shards with a leased conditional update, enqueue runs in priority lanes and advance next_run_time for recurring jobs
Hand jobs due before the next polling window directly to a Task Scheduler
Execute runs idempotently on Workers, record their status, retry with exponential backoff and park runs that keep failing in a Dead Letter Queue
nonFunctional: ~100 M scheduled jobs; ~10 K runs/s at the top of each hour (~10× the average)
Start runs within ~1 s of their scheduled time
Never lose a job: at-least-once execution that survives a Task Scheduler or Worker failure
constraints: Web Servers never run jobs; runs reach Workers only through the Message Queue
Claim jobs with a conditional update and a lease, never a plain read followed by a write
Make every job idempotent, because a re-delivered run may execute twice
capacity: ~100 M jobs; ~1 K runs/s on average, ~10 K runs/s at the top of the hour
Each scheduler polls its shards for jobs due in the next few seconds
Workers autoscale on queue depth to absorb the hourly spikes
specs.tradeoff: Polling SQL for due jobs is simple and durable but adds database load and up to one polling interval of delay, which is why jobs due very soon skip the poll. At-least-once delivery never loses a run but may run one twice, so jobs must be idempotent; exactly-once execution would need far more coordination. Sharding the schedulers scales claiming but needs a coordination service to reassign shards when one dies.
specs.bonus: Connect Task Scheduler → ZooKeeper / etcd for shard ownership and leader election, and add Monitoring for schedule lag and failures.

topologyRules.message: Don't call Workers from the API — runs go through the schedulers and the queue.
Deliver runs from the schedulers to Workers through the Message Queue.

resilienceRules.message: A single scheduler is a single point of failure — run several, each owning shards.
Run at least two Workers so runs continue after one fails.
Connect the run queue to a Dead Letter Queue for runs that keep failing.

hints: Start with Client → Load Balancer → Web Server, and Web Server → SQL Database for job definitions, next_run_time and run history.

Connect Web Server → Task Scheduler for jobs due very soon, and Task Scheduler → SQL Database to claim due jobs with a lease. Then wire Task Scheduler → Message Queue → Worker, with Worker → SQL Database for run status and a Dead Letter Queue on the queue.

Run two Web Servers, two Task Schedulers and two Workers. Each Web Server reaches SQL, both schedulers and Monitoring; each scheduler reaches SQL, the queue and ZooKeeper / etcd; the queue feeds both Workers and the Dead Letter Queue, and each Worker writes SQL.
